channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You struggle to change your mind when you feel threatened.
item.description: System justification theory suggests you defend the status quo even when it works against your own interests.

item.title: You spend money differently depending on where it comes from.
item.description: Mental accounting explains why you treat a $100 windfall differently than $100 from your salary.

item.title: You view your own mistakes as bad luck.
item.description: The claim attributes both halves of the actor-observer asymmetry to the Fundamental Attribution Error.

item.title: You feel an immediate desire for what is forbidden.
item.description: Psychological reactance occurs when you perceive a threat to your freedom of choice.

item.title: You judge strangers as kinder based purely on appearance.
item.description: The halo effect is the tendency for an overall impression of a person to influence your feelings about their character.

item.title: You overestimate how much people notice your minor behaviors.
item.description: The spotlight effect is your tendency to feel that your actions are being observed by everyone.

item.title: You derive your self-worth by comparing yourself to peers.
item.description: Social comparison theory posits that you evaluate your own abilities and opinions by comparing them to others.

item.title: You weight negative information more heavily than positive feedback.
item.description: The negativity bias causes you to focus on threats and failures far more than gains.

item.title: You remember details better if they concern your own personality.
item.description: The self-reference effect demonstrates that information encoded in relation to the self is often recalled more effectively than information processed through structural or semantic tasks.

item.title: You are less likely to help someone if you are in a crowd.
item.description: The bystander effect demonstrates that the presence of others reduces your perceived personal responsibility to intervene.

item.title: You remember past events more fondly than you felt them at the time.
item.description: Rosy retrospection is the tendency to assign more positive attributes to past experiences as they fade from memory.

item.title: You assume you are less likely than others to experience misfortune.
item.description: The optimism bias is your tendency to believe that your future will be more positive than the evidence supports.

item.title: You fail to see clear objects when your focus is locked.
item.description: Inattentional blindness describes your inability to perceive visible stimuli when your attention is directed elsewhere.

item.title: You become more likable after making a small, visible mistake.
item.description: The pratfall effect suggests that a minor error makes a highly competent individual more appealing, but can decrease the appeal of someone perceived as mediocre.

item.title: You exaggerate the importance of your current life focus.
item.description: The focusing illusion occurs when you place too much weight on one aspect of life while ignoring others.

item.title: You mistake easy thinking for the truth.
item.description: Cognitive fluency is the phenomenon where you evaluate information as more truthful if it is easy to process.

item.title: Your choice changes based on how the risk is framed.
item.description: The framing effect, as demonstrated by Tversky and Kahneman (1981), shows that people react to choices differently depending on whether they are presented as gains or losses.

item.title: You assume the worst when others act neutrally.
item.description: Hostile attribution bias causes people to interpret ambiguous social cues as intentionally aggressive.

item.title: You work less when you are in a group.
item.description: Latané, Williams, and Harkins (1979) demonstrated social loafing by measuring tasks like shouting and clapping to isolate motivational loss from coordination loss.

item.title: A small favor makes you say yes to big ones.
item.description: The foot-in-the-door technique increases compliance by securing a small, trivial commitment before asking for a substantial one.

item.title: You judge objects as more valuable if they are scarce.
item.description: The scarcity heuristic leads people to place a higher value on items that are perceived as rare or difficult to obtain.

item.title: Asking if you will act makes you more likely to.
item.description: The mere measurement effect describes a phenomenon where measuring intentions may influence subsequent behavior, though this effect is highly context-dependent.

item.title: Your judgment is skewed by what you saw before.
item.description: The contrast effect describes how the perception of an object is changed by its comparison to a preceding object, a phenomenon explored in social psychology regarding attractiveness judgments.

item.title: You are terrible at predicting your feelings in a cold state.
item.description: The hot-cold empathy gap prevents you from accurately anticipating how you will behave when you are hungry, angry, or excited.

item.title: Your brain tracks background noise until your name is spoken.
item.description: The cocktail party effect describes your ability to focus your attention on one voice while ignoring other background stimuli.

item.title: Your first impression of a price anchors every later decision.
item.description: The anchoring effect is a cognitive bias where the first piece of information offered influences all subsequent judgments.

item.title: You believe you are better than you actually are.
item.description: A 1981 study found that 93% of the US student sample surveyed rated their driving skills as above the median.

item.title: You remember unusual details better than common ones.
item.description: The bizarreness effect suggests that bizarre items are sometimes recalled better than common ones, though researchers argue this is a result of distinctiveness rather than the inherent bizarreness of the material.

item.title: You misremember your past choices as smarter than they were.
item.description: Choice-supportive bias occurs when you remember your previous decisions as better and more rational than they were at the time.

item.title: You find deep meaning in vague, generic descriptions.
item.description: The Barnum effect is a specific instance of the broader concept of subjective validation.

item.title: A minor lapse in control leads to a total collapse.
item.description: The 'what-the-hell' effect describes how a small violation of a goal leads to the abandonment of that goal entirely.

item.title: You repeat a false statement until you believe it.
item.description: The illusory truth effect describes the tendency to believe repeated information is more credible, a phenomenon first established by Hasher, Goldstein, and Toppino in 1977.

item.title: You systematically overestimate how much you know about topics.
item.description: The overconfidence effect is a bias where subjective confidence in judgments often exceeds objective accuracy, though this depends significantly on task difficulty.

item.title: You judge risk by how easily you recall stories.
item.description: The availability heuristic causes you to overestimate the probability of events that are emotionally vivid or recently publicized.

item.title: Disconfirming evidence can strengthen your initial incorrect belief.
item.description: The 'backfire effect' was proposed in 2010 to describe people doubling down on beliefs, but subsequent large-scale research has failed to replicate this as a common phenomenon.

item.title: A tiny, unsolicited gift alters your future decision-making process.
item.description: The reciprocity norm creates an internal discomfort that compels you to repay favors.

item.title: Your brain actively ignores evidence that contradicts your view.
item.description: Confirmation bias involves selectively processing information to support existing beliefs.

item.title: You blame circumstances for failure but yourself for success.
item.description: The self-serving bias is observed as a pattern of attribution, but its status as a defense mechanism for self-esteem is debated.

item.title: You subconsciously blame victims to preserve your sense of safety.
item.description: The just-world hypothesis suggests people blame victims to believe the world is inherently fair.

item.title: You buy more when a useless option is added.
item.description: The inclusion of an asymmetrically dominated decoy makes a target option look more attractive.

item.title: You assume others see your internal nerves clearly.
item.description: People underestimate their ability to conceal their internal emotional states.

item.title: You avoid action to prevent the possibility of regret.
item.description: The omission bias is the tendency to judge harmful actions as worse than equally harmful instances of inaction.

item.title: Your current mood dictates your tolerance for risk.
item.description: The affect heuristic means that your feelings act as a shortcut for making complex decisions.

item.title: You believe you control things that are purely random.
item.description: The illusion of control causes you to overestimate your influence over chance-based outcomes.

item.title: You only remember the beginning and the end.
item.description: The serial position effect demonstrates that recall is typically highest for the first and last items in a sequence.

item.title: You mistake others' circumstances for their personality traits.
item.description: The fundamental attribution error describes your tendency to blame others' actions on character rather than the environment.

item.title: Your brain prioritizes bad news over good news.
item.description: The negativity bias means that human cognition reacts more strongly to unpleasant stimuli than to positive ones of equal intensity.

item.title: A single new purchase triggers an endless cycle of consumption.
item.description: Grant McCracken's 1988 book 'Culture and Consumption' introduced the 'Diderot effect' as a sociological concept, interpreting Diderot's 1769 essay to explain consumer behavior.

item.title: A single positive trait tricks you into seeing perfection.
item.description: A 1920 study found that when soldiers were rated high in one physical area, they were systematically rated high in intelligence and leadership too.

item.title: You feel worse because you imagined a better outcome.
item.description: A 1997 review article by Neal Roese synthesizes the established connection between upward counterfactuals and regret, a relationship previously identified in earlier empirical research.
